title: After the Gold Rush: The Promise of Evolution of PFAS-Eating Bacteria
description: Microbiologists keep sampling PFAS-polluted sites to hunt for PFAS-degrading bacteria, but evolution gives microbes little reason to select for that trait. A case for looking somewhere else entirely.
body:
*The holy grail of microbial bioremediation is to find bacteria that break down the nearly indestructible per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) or “forever chemicals”. To this end, researchers have been trying to find PFAS-eating bacteria from PFAS-polluted environments, because this is the classical method in microbiology. But PFAS are different from most other organic pollutants and there is very little reason why evolution would allow for efficient PFAS-degraders to emerge. This begs the question: **Why?** Why do microbiologists prefer to go to PFAS-polluted sites, in the hopes of finding good bacteria that degrade forever chemicals?*

Historically, microbiologists have looked to environments that were already contaminated with the pollutant they want to degrade with microorganisms. We bring a shovel, drill, container, or whatever we need to bring the environmental sample back to the lab. Back home in the lab, we often try to find microorganisms in the soil sample (or whatever the sample consists of) that can eat the pollutant. This is often done by feeding the microorganisms with only one food: the chemical that we want to have degraded. While there are many variations to the setup in the lab, the end goal and dream is often the same: to find a microorganism (be it bacterial or fungal) that can use the pollutant, in this case PFAS, as its ONLY food source. This has worked well for other chemicals; pesticides, petrochemicals, pharmaceuticals, organic solvents, etc. A case that I personally find fascinating is the story of lindane- and pentachlorophenol; or their short names HCH and PCP. These chemicals were used heavily from the 1930s and 1940s as pesticides and as heavy-duty wood preservative for e.g. utility poles, and lindane is still used to battle hair lice in people in some parts of the world. Both chemicals consist of a so-called benzene ring and have 5 or 6 chlorine atoms, where hydrogens would sit in a natural molecule. This makes them really tough to degrade by microorganisms, so they stay in the environment for a long time as pollutants with toxic effects to organisms (Crawford et al., 2007).

![Pentachlorophenol and hexachlorocyclohexane structures, alongside a head louse](fig-hch-pcp-louse.jpg)

*Pentachlorophenol (PCP; left) and hexachlorocyclohexane/lindane (HCH; right) are two related man-made chemicals for which evolution has developed degradation pathways in bacteria, allowing microorganisms to grow using them as their carbon- and energy source. Lindane has been used (and still in use in some countries) to combat head lice, but has been mostly phased out due to neurotoxicity. All pictures are from Wikipedia.*

However, a range of studies showed in the 2000’s and 2010’s that in the course of a few decades, specific microorganisms had rearranged their genetics through evolution to form a new patchwork of DNA that had enabled them to degrade these chemicals (Copley, 2000; Copley et al., 2012; Sangwan et al., 2014; Pearce et al., 2015). While toxic to many organisms, HCH and PCP can make a good food source for adapted bacteria. This gives evolution a reason for reorganizing and optimizing the genetic material leading to degradation of HCH and PCP: positive selection!

But in the case of PFAS, something is different. The perfluorinated versions of PFAS (all carbon-hydrogen bonds replaced by carbon-fluoride bonds e.g. PFOA and PFOS) are among the most difficult to degrade of this huge class of chemicals and the ones that we often prioritize to find biodegradation of. However, these are frankly terrible snacks for microorganisms. They consist mainly of carbon-fluorine bonds that are the strongest bonds in organic chemistry (O’Hagan, 2008). In lay terms, this means that microorganisms will spend more energy digesting the chemical than they can gain (Wackett, 2025).

![Structure of perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA)](fig-pfoa.jpg)

*Perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) is a PFAS of major concern and one of the first chemicals of the class to be subject to regulations. The company 3M started phasing out PFOA in 2002 voluntarily, with large-scale production running since 1947. PFOA and other PFAS have been widely used in anything from industrial production facilities to raincoats, building materials, children’s toys, etc. It has a wide range of health- and environmental effects (Buck et al., 2011).*

Imagine eating a sandwich but you spend more calories processing it in the gut than you can obtain from it. And it poisons you in the process.

Moreover, toxic fluoride is released during degradation of PFAS, poisoning the bacteria and its enzymes (Baker et al., 2012; Wackett, 2021). So as a bacterium, you would generally not gain any advantage in PFAS degradation and furthermore will poison yourself and your near environment with toxic fluoride. In the end, a single celled organism that has the capability to degrade PFAS will most likely have a disadvantage in life over their siblings that happen to not degrade it (e.g. through random mutations). What does this imply? Evolution should select AGAINST PFAS degrading-microbes in almost all cases (Wackett, 2024).

So why are microbiologists obsessed with looking for bugs in PFAS-polluted sites, such as fields used for firefighting exercises where aqueous film-forming foam (AFFF) has been used extensively? I would argue that it is a combination of historical reasons and a pipedream.

As for HCH, PCP, and other pollutants where looking for microbes that want to eat the chemicals as the ONLY food source, researchers are globally looking for bugs that can eat PFAS. I have done the same in several projects – even knowing that evolution of efficient PFAS degraders is unlikely. I might as well have sampled sewage water with no PFAS instead field site with heavy contamination (actually there are good reasons for doing this, which I will not go into here).

![Sampling PFAS-polluted soil at a Danish airport](cover.jpg)

*Historically, microbiologists have been sampling polluted environments to find bacteria that can eat the given chemicals. This will likely not work for PFAS in most cases. The picture shows myself sampling PFAS-polluted soil from an airport in Denmark, where PFAS-rich Aqueous Film-Forming Foam (AFFF) has been used extensively for training firefighting.*

In these years, many research publications are coming out that claim highly efficient degradation of PFAS by a single bacterial species. Many even claim that PFAS can be provided as the only food source for these bacteria. This is an extraordinary claim due to our knowledge about chemistry, physics, and microbial metabolism (Skinner et al., 2025). As famous astronomer Carl Sagan said in 1980 in his TV-series Cosmos:

*“Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence” – Carl Sagan*

*“Bacteria eating PFAS (especially the perfluorinated) as their only source of carbon and energy is an extraordinary claim!” – Tue Kjærgaard Nielsen*

Caution should be applied when accepting studies making such claims. I will not refer to specific studies here, since such things belong in a peer-reviewed publication and not a blog post. The reasons why I question several research papers claiming PFAS biodegradation are technical, elaborate, and outside the scope of this post.

So what’s the alternative to sampling PFAS-polluted sites, where evolution of PFAS-degrading bacteria is unlikely, since the chemicals are terrible and toxic food sources for the bugs? Well, **toxic** may give us a clue towards where we should actually look for PFAS-degrading microorganisms. We are starting to discover how some PFAS poisons very specific (and niche) microorganisms. A bacterium whose lifestyle is fundamentally disturbed also has a motif to detoxify the PFAS! This could be degradation (or other non-degrading mechanisms). We are starting to discover how PFAS can poison very specific microbial functions: photosynthesis, nitrogen-cycling, and others.

Imagine you are an algae and your photosynthesis gets stopped by PFAS: no more energy and no more carbon from CO2: bad news!

In a pre-print article (not yet peer reviewed), we described how some cyanobacteria, which humans usually find terribly annoying since they produce toxins that prevent us from swimming on a hot summer day, carry genetic signatures indicating potential for PFAS degradation (Forouzandeh et al., 2025). It was previously shown that some PFAS can inhibit photosynthesis in cyanobacteria (Wu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2025); bad news when your life depends on this trait! So did cyanobacteria recently evolve to detoxify PFAS through degradation? This is still ongoing research.

In another case, some PFAS shows potential for inhibiting essential functions in nitrogen-cycling microorganisms: functions that are fundamental for their lifestyle (Fu et al., 2025). Poisoning such essential functions imposes a real positive selection for degradation or other means of detoxification that evolution can actually work with! My personal opinion is that we should look towards such niches for potential PFAS-degrading microorganisms. In other words, we need two ingredients:

- A motive: inhibition of essential function by PFAS
- A weapon: an enzyme that degrades (or detoxifies) PFAS

TL;DR: I argue that PFAS-pollution in a given environmental site does not mean that the site is a good place to sample for PFAS-degrading microorganisms, due to a lack of positive selection for evolution.
